Twenty-two stages, in the order to do them. Each one names what you can do afterwards and why it matters for Alaap, then puts in front of you everything that stage needs: the Alaap guide's own sections, the TrenTorch module you build, a diagram, the relevant architecture, where Accelerate practises it, and one exit check with its answer.

About 83 h in all: Alaap guide hours as the guide states them, TrenTorch at about 1.5 hours a module. Milestones follow Accelerate's roadmap. The guide's own target, for reference:

Target: ~5 h/week, ~13 weeks, ~65 hours. Starting point assumed: you know ML theory and algorithms. You do not know PyTorch, and you have not worked with audio. End state: you can read every paper this project rests on, argue with its backend choices, and change an experiment and trust the result.

    Exit check Why is the TTS model never trained, and what would break if it were?

    Show the answer

    All the learning lives in the mapper, which produces a vector the frozen model already knows how to consume. Train the TTS and the vector space moves under every stored identity, so every minted voice drifts, and the independent drift and consistency judges stop meaning anything.

    Stage 1

    Sound as data: sampling and Nyquist

    about 2 h
    • Alaap guide 2.1

    Practised in Accelerate Week 3, Sampling and Nyquist   On the map Sampling and Nyquist

    After this you can Say what a sample rate buys you, find the Nyquist cliff on a real spectrum, and explain why analysing audio at the wrong rate moves every frequency.

    Why it matters for Alaap Alaap's audio lives at four sample rates: corpus 24 kHz, WavLM 16 kHz, MioCodec 44.1 kHz, Sarvam 22.05 kHz. Mixing them up once reversed an experiment's result.

    From the Alaap guide, Part 2: Sound as data weeks 3–5, 12 h

    After this you can read alaap/acoustics.py and say what every function measures and how it could be wrong.

    Guide 2.1 Sampling and the time domain 2 h

    Sample rate, Nyquist, bit depth, why 16 kHz / 22.05 kHz / 24 kHz / 44.1 kHz all appear here.

    Intuition a waveform is a very long list of air-pressure readings. Nyquist says you can represent frequencies up to half your sample rate and nothing above.

    Why it matters this project's audio lives at four sample rates — corpus 24 kHz, WavLM 16 kHz, MioCodec 44.1 kHz, Sarvam 22.05 kHz — and analysing one at another's rate puts every frequency off by a ratio. That happened in S21 phase B and reversed a result.

    Do: load a clip at 24 kHz, resample to 16 kHz, plot both spectra. Find the cliff.

    Exit check A clip recorded at 24 kHz is resampled to 16 kHz. What happens to a component at 10 kHz, and why?

    Show the answer

    It is removed. At 16 kHz the Nyquist limit is 8 kHz, so the resampler's low-pass filter cuts everything above it; without that filter the 10 kHz energy would alias down to 6 kHz. That is the cliff you find on the plot.

    Stage 2

    Source and filter: what describes a voice

    about 3 h
    • Alaap guide 2.3

    Practised in Accelerate Week 5, The source-filter model   On the map The source-filter model

    After this you can Separate the glottal buzz (F0) from the vocal-tract tube (formants), and map each of Alaap's measurements onto one side or the other.

    Why it matters for Alaap Alaap's identity axes are exactly this split: f0_mean measures the source, vtl_cm and the formants measure the filter, and spectral_tilt was meant to measure the source's shape but partly reads pitch.

    Guide 2.3 The source–filter model 3 h

    Glottal source (pitch, F0) vs vocal-tract filter (formants). Why they are separable and why that separation is the whole basis of describing a voice.

    Intuition the vocal folds make a buzz at F0. The mouth and throat are a tube that resonates at certain frequencies — formants. Change the buzz, same person. Change the tube, different person.

    This is the single most important idea in Part 2. f0_mean measures the source; vtl_cm and the formants measure the filter; spectral_tilt is supposed to measure the source's spectral shape and — as S21 found — partly measures the buzz rate instead.

    Also in the architecture 8 · The attribute taxonomy

    Exit check Two recordings of the same person, one speaking and one singing higher. Which measurements should move, and which should not?

    Show the answer

    The source moves: F0 goes up. The filter should not: vocal-tract length and the formant pattern belong to the tube, which is the same person. A measurement that moves with F0 when it claims to measure the tube, as spectral tilt partly did, is confounded.

    Guide 1.1 The tensor

    Shapes, dtypes, devices, broadcasting, view/reshape/permute, indexing.

    Intuition a tensor is a numpy array that remembers where it came from. That memory is autograd.

    Exit check A (32, 1, 80) tensor is added to an (80,) tensor. What is the result's shape, and what did broadcasting do?

    Show the answer

    (32, 1, 80). The (80,) tensor is treated as (1, 1, 80) and virtually repeated along the first two axes without copying memory, then added element by element.

    Reflection questions from the module (5)
    1. Computational Cost Comparison. ReLU is the most popular activation function in hidden layers. Given what you implemented, why is ReLU computationally cheaper than Sigmoid or GELU?
    2. Numerical Stability. Look at your Softmax implementation. Why did we subtract the maximum value before computing exponentials?
    3. Sparsity and Efficiency. ReLU creates "sparsity" by zeroing negative values. Why might having many zero activations be beneficial for computation?
    4. Activation Selection for Different Stages. Why do we typically use different activations for hidden stages vs. output stages of a computation?
    5. The "Dying ReLU" Problem. If ReLU outputs 0 for some inputs, those inputs get no signal passed through -- they effectively "die." What situations might cause this, and why is it a problem?

    Reflection questions from the module (5)
    1. Parameter Scaling and Memory. Consider three different network architectures for MNIST (28x28 = 784 input features, 10 output classes):
    2. Dropout Training vs Inference. You have a Dropout layer with p=0.5 in your network. During training, we scale surviving values by 1/(1-p) = 2.0.
    3. Weight Initialization Trade-offs. We initialize weights with scale = sqrt(1/in_features) (LeCun-style). For Linear(1000, 10), how does this compare to Linear(10, 1000)?
    4. Layer Ordering Effects. In a typical layer block, we compose: Linear -> Activation -> Dropout. What happens if you change the order to: Linear -> Dropout -> Activation?
    5. Production Deployment Memory. You're deploying a 3-layer network (784->256->128->10) to a mobile device with 10MB free memory.

    Guide 1.3 nn.Module

    __init__ vs forward, parameters vs buffers, train()/eval(), state_dict.

    Why it matters here model.eval() and torch.no_grad() appear in every experiment in this repo. Know exactly what each turns off — they are not the same thing.

    Exit check Dropout with p = 0.5 scales surviving activations by 2 during training. What does it do at eval time, and why the scaling?

    Show the answer

    Nothing: at eval every unit passes through unscaled. Scaling by 1/(1-p) during training keeps the expected activation the same in both modes, so the next layer sees the same magnitudes whether or not dropout is on.

    Exit check With softmax and cross-entropy together, what is the gradient with respect to the logits?

    Show the answer

    p minus the one-hot target. It stays large while the prediction is wrong, however confident, which is why this pairing does not stall the way sigmoid plus squared error does.

    Exit check Samples are stored ordered by speaker. What goes wrong if you train without shuffling?

    Show the answer

    Each batch holds one speaker, so gradients chase that speaker and then the next: training oscillates, and the model forgets earlier speakers. Shuffling makes each batch a fair sample of the whole set.

    Reflection questions from the module (5)
    1. Computational Graph Memory. A 10-layer neural network processes a single sample. Each layer performs matrix multiplication (matmul) and addition (bias). How much memory does the computation graph use compared to just storing the weights?
    2. Gradient Accumulation. A weight matrix is shared between two computation paths in a network (like a tied-weights architecture). Why does gradient accumulation (`grad = grad + new_grad`) save memory during training? What's the trade-off?
    3. Backward Pass Cost. A forward pass through a 3-layer MLP takes 10ms. Is the backward pass faster, slower, or the same speed as the forward pass? Why?
    4. Graph Retention. You're training a language model that processes sequences of varying lengths. When should you call `.zero_grad()`? What happens if you forget?
    5. Production Pattern. PyTorch and TensorFlow use `requires_grad` flags instead of always tracking gradients for every tensor. Why? What's the performance benefit of making gradient tracking opt-in?

    Guide 1.2 Autograd

    requires_grad, the graph, backward(), torch.no_grad(), why .detach() exists.

    Intuition the graph is built forward as a side effect of computing, then walked backward. Nothing is symbolic; it is a recorded tape.

    Exit check y = x @ W. Given the gradient of the loss with respect to y, what are the gradients for x and W?

    Show the answer

    grad_x = grad_y @ W.T and grad_W = x.T @ grad_y. Two matmuls backward for one forward, which is why the backward pass costs roughly twice the forward.

    Exit check What happens if you forget zero_grad() between steps?

    Show the answer

    Gradients accumulate across steps, so each update applies the sum of every previous gradient: steps grow and training diverges. Accumulation is useful on purpose, for a large effective batch, but only when you zero it every N steps.

    Stage 9

    The same things, in real PyTorch

    about 3 h
    • Alaap guide 1.5

    On the map Part 1's exit checklist

    After this you can Map every TrenTorch piece to its PyTorch name, and pass Part 1's exit checklist on a real Alaap model: WavLM's hidden states.

    Why it matters for Alaap TrenTorch taught the mechanism; Alaap is written in PyTorch. This stage closes that gap, including the lesson that out-of-memory is sometimes system RAM, not VRAM.

    Guide 1.5 The things that bite

    • CPU vs CUDA, and .to(device) on both model and data
    • memory: activations dominate, not weights
    • float32 vs bfloat16
    • why a model that "fits in VRAM" still OOMs

    This repo's own version of that lesson: loading two models in one process segfaults on a 15.7 GB box while the 6 GB GPU sits at 614 MiB. It is system RAM, not VRAM. See HANDOFF.md §8b.

    Do in this repo, no training required:
    import torch, torchaudio
m = torchaudio.pipelines.WAVLM_BASE_PLUS.get_model().eval()
x = torch.randn(1, 16000)          # 1 second at 16 kHz
with torch.no_grad():
    hs, _ = m.extract_features(x, num_layers=12)
print(len(hs), hs[0].shape)

    Then explain, out loud: why 12 tensors? What are the three dimensions of each? Why no_grad()?

    Check Why does hs[0].shape[1] change when you change the input length, and what is the ratio? (This is the frame rate, and it is the first properly "audio" idea.)

    Exit check model.eval() and torch.no_grad() are both used in every Alaap experiment. What does each switch off?

    Show the answer

    eval() changes layer behaviour: dropout stops dropping and batch norm uses its running statistics. no_grad() stops recording the graph, so no activations are kept for backward and memory falls. They are independent, and inference wants both.

    Exit check Batch normalisation has two separate effects. Name them.

    Show the answer

    It normalises each channel's activations to zero mean and unit variance using the batch, which steadies and speeds up training. And because batch statistics are noisy, it adds a regularising noise. At eval it swaps batch statistics for running ones, which is why eval() matters.

    Stage 11

    The rest of sound: frequency, and how estimators lie

    about 7 h
    • Alaap guide 2.2
    • Alaap guide 2.4

    After this you can Read a spectrogram's time and frequency resolution from its parameters, and read alaap/acoustics.py saying what each function measures and how it can be wrong.

    Why it matters for Alaap Every attribute Alaap captions is produced by these estimators. If measure() is wrong, the caption, the mapper and the adherence score are all wrong together and nothing complains.

    Guide 2.2 The frequency domain 3 h

    DFT/FFT, window functions, the STFT, the spectrogram, mel scale, MFCCs.

    Intuition the STFT is "run an FFT on a sliding window". Every parameter is a trade: a long window gives fine frequency resolution and blurry time; a short one, the reverse.

    Read any good DSP intro; Smith's Mathematics of the DFT if you want rigour.

    Do in this repo:

    import librosa, numpy as np
S = np.abs(librosa.stft(wav, n_fft=2048, hop_length=512))

    n_fft=2048 at 24 kHz gives what frequency resolution? What time resolution? Both numbers appear in spectral_tilt and both matter.

    Guide 2.4 The estimators, and how each one lies 4 h

    Read alaap/acoustics.py top to bottom. Every docstring is a lesson someone paid for.

    function the trap
    f0_track pYIN; octave errors on creaky voice
    voiced_mask an energy+ZCR VAD, not a periodicity detector; structurally capped near 0.60 and bimodal
    formants LPC order and analysis rate; run at ~2× max formant, not native
    vocal_tract_length never average through F2 — it is vowel-dependent
    spectral_tilt OLS over linear FFT bins puts 43% of leverage on 27 bins
    speaking_rate needs text; silently NaN without it; g2p-en does not raise on Devanagari

    Read the project skill .claude/skills/speech-feature-pitfalls/SKILL.md — it is the compressed version of everything above, written from real failures here.

    Check Why does a 250 Hz voice read a flatter spectral tilt than a 90 Hz voice with an identical spectral envelope? (Answer in experiments/S21-spectral-tilt/RESULTS.md.)

    Also in the architecture 8 · The attribute taxonomy · 6 · Reversibility — the property that makes captions checkable

    Exit check At 24 kHz with n_fft = 2048 and hop 512, what are the frequency and time resolutions?

    Show the answer

    Frequency: 24000 / 2048, about 11.7 Hz per bin. Time: 512 / 24000, about 21 ms between frames, with each window 85 ms long. Finer frequency costs blurrier time, and the reverse.

    Stage 12

    Speaker identity: embeddings that recognise people

    about 5 h
    • Alaap guide 3.1
    • Alaap guide 3.2

    Practised in Accelerate Week 3, Vectors and matrices: cosine similarity · Week 4, Embeddings and attention: where embeddings come from   On the map Part 3, speaker identity

    After this you can Explain how a speaker embedding is made, why it is invariant to channel, and why verification thresholds must be fitted in-domain.

    Why it matters for Alaap ECAPA is trained to ignore channel and quality, so it can recognise you down a bad line. That is exactly why Alaap uses it as the independent judge for identity and never for quality.

    From the Alaap guide, Part 3: Speaker identity weeks 6–7, 10 h

    After this you can read the three papers the whole architecture rests on, and explain why a speaker embedding is not just "an embedding".

    Guide 3.1 From i-vectors to ECAPA 3 h

    Read
    • Snyder et al., "X-Vectors: Robust DNN Embeddings for Speaker Recognition", ICASSP 2018
    • Desplanques et al., "ECAPA-TDNN: Emphasized Channel Attention, Propagation and Aggregation in TDNN Based Speaker Verification", Interspeech 2020

    Intuition train a network to tell speakers apart; throw away the classifier; the penultimate layer is now a speaker embedding. Everything downstream inherits whatever that training made it invariant to.

    Why it matters here — and it is a rule, not a detail

    ECAPA is trained to be INVARIANT to channel and quality, so it can recognise you down a bad phone line. That is exactly why it must never be used to measure quality. It is the project's independent judge for identity, and nothing else.

    Guide 3.2 Cosine, EER, and calibration 2 h

    Cosine similarity, thresholds, EER, and why a threshold from a paper does not transfer.

    Do read alaap/metrics.py's CALIBRATION and E4's results. C_same = 0.6988, C_diff = 0.2011. Then answer: why must these be fit in-domain? (E4 measured that doing so halves EER.)

    Also in the architecture 12 · Module map

    Exit check Why does fitting C_same and C_diff in-domain halve the equal error rate?

    Show the answer

    Cosine scores depend on the corpus, channel and language. A threshold from a paper sits in the wrong place for Alaap's audio, so it trades errors badly; fitted on Alaap's own same-speaker and different-speaker pairs, it sits where the two distributions actually cross.

    Stage 13

    Is the space navigable?

    about 5 h
    • Alaap guide 3.3
    • Alaap guide 3.4

    Practised in Accelerate Week 3, Vectors and matrices: eigenvectors   On the map The navigability papers

    After this you can Argue, from three papers, that a speaker embedding space can be sampled and interpolated, and say what goes wrong in sparse regions and past the shell.

    Why it matters for Alaap This is the intellectual core of the project: if the space could not be navigated, Tower A would not be worth training.

    Guide 3.3 Is the space navigable? 3 h

    This is the intellectual core of the project. Three papers, all in SOURCES.md:
    arXiv:1806.04558 §3.6 — Jia et al., NeurIPS 2018 random unit-hypersphere vectors → MOS 3.65, "as natural as real speakers". The manifold is navigable.
    arXiv:2111.05095 §6.2 — TacoSpawn discriminative d-vector spaces resist parametric priors (g2s 0.35 vs s2s 0.20). Learned spaces do not.
    arXiv:2207.04834 §5.1.1 — Meyer et al. the collapse and its fix. Per-dim rescaling: GVD −6.50 → −0.14. Dimension ranges span three orders of magnitude.

    Intuition for the third one: if one dimension ranges over ±80 and another over ±0.5, then an unweighted MSE loss is entirely about the first dimension. Every voice collapses onto the same one. Rescale per dimension or the model learns nothing.

    Guide 3.4 Moving through the space 2 h

    Interpolation vs extrapolation; SLERP vs LERP; sparse regions.
    arXiv:2106.05762 1,225 pairwise interpolations, WER 6.42–7.35%. Interpolation works.
    arXiv:2310.03538 "extrapolation is not particularly meaningful"
    arXiv:2508.19210 SLERP not LERP — preserves unit norm
    arXiv:2005.08601 sparse-region averaging costs +60% relative WER

    Check Why does mint(novelty=0.7) produce voices closer to the centre of the space, not further from it? (S9. It is not obvious, and the experiment retracted a claim over it.)

    Architecture: 7 · Speaker-space geometry Open in the architecture tab

    You cannot treat a speaker embedding space as isotropic. This is invariant I1, and ignoring it collapses every identity onto one voice.

    Exit check Why SLERP rather than linear interpolation between two speaker vectors?

    Show the answer

    Real speakers sit on a shell at roughly constant norm. A straight line between two points on a sphere cuts inside it, where the norm shrinks and the voice drifts toward the average. SLERP stays on the shell.

    Exit check Where do the numbers in an embedding table come from?

    Show the answer

    They are ordinary weights: a (vocabulary x dimension) matrix, initialised randomly and updated by gradient descent. Looking up a token is selecting a row, which is the same as multiplying a one-hot vector by the matrix.

    Exit check Why divide QK^T by the square root of d_k?

    Show the answer

    With unit-variance entries, a dot product of d_k terms has variance d_k, so scores grow with dimension. Large scores push softmax into saturation where its gradients vanish. Dividing by the square root of d_k keeps the variance near one.

    How a TTS model actually works

    about 10 h

    On the map Parts 4 to 6

    After this you can Read the model card of any open TTS system and predict whether it can serve Alaap's architecture.

    Why it matters for Alaap Codecs turn audio into integers, which is why modern TTS is a language model, and why Alaap can decode forty voices for the price of one.

    From the Alaap guide, Part 4: How a TTS model actually works weeks 8–9, 10 h

    After this you can read the model card of any open TTS system and predict whether it can serve this architecture.

    Guide 4.1 The shape of the field 2 h

    Autoregressive vs non-autoregressive; two-stage (text→tokens→waveform) vs end-to-end.

    Read Kim et al., "VITS: Conditional Variational Autoencoder with Adversarial Learning for End-to-End Text-to-Speech", 2021. It is the clean end-to-end baseline everything else is a reaction to.

    Guide 4.2 Neural audio codecs 3 h the key unlock

    Read
    • Zeghidour et al., "SoundStream: An End-to-End Neural Audio Codec", 2021
    • Défossez et al., "High Fidelity Neural Audio Compression" (EnCodec), 2022
    • Mentzer et al., "Finite Scalar Quantization: VQ-VAE Made Simple", 2023 — FSQ, which is what MioCodec uses

    Intuition a codec learns to turn a waveform into a short sequence of integers and back. Once audio is integers, a language model can generate it. That is why modern TTS is a language model.

    Why FSQ specifically: it replaces a learned codebook with a fixed grid — quantise each of 5 dimensions to [8,8,8,5,5] levels, giving 12 800 combinations, no codebook collapse, no auxiliary losses.

    And the trap, which cost this project a week: two FSQ codecs with the same levels share no codebook. Every index is valid in both. Nothing raises. You get fluent speech saying different words. Diagram 10 in architecture.html.

    Guide 4.3 Self-supervised speech representations 2 h

    Read Chen et al., "WavLM: Large-Scale Self-Supervised Pre-Training for Full Stack Speech Processing", 2022. HuBERT if you want the predecessor.

    Intuition train on unlabelled audio by masking and predicting. Different layers end up encoding different things — early layers pitch and speaker, middle layers phonetic content.

    Why it matters here the naturalness gate is distance to the real-speech manifold in WavLM features, and which layer you pool changes what you measure. Layer 0 correlates with F0 at −0.578, which is the DNSMOS trap in disguise. See S20b and S23.

    Guide 4.4 Flow matching and diffusion, enough to argue 3 h

    Read Lipman et al., "Flow Matching for Generative Modeling", 2023. Skim the maths; get the picture.

    Intuition diffusion learns to reverse noise step by step. Flow matching learns a velocity field that transports noise to data along a straight-ish path — fewer steps, same destination.

    The one A/B that matters here, from SOURCES.md:

    arXiv:2406.08812, Interspeech 2024 — flow matching wins fidelity (FAD 3.559 vs 5.244) and loses adherence (SRCC 0.60 vs 0.74). A hybrid is best. The trade is bidirectional — which is why this project's S3 plans MDN first.

    This split is what makes the Indic experiments cheap. It is also where the project's most expensive bug lived.

    Exit check Two FSQ codecs both use levels [8, 8, 8, 5, 5]. Why can you not feed one's tokens to the other's decoder?

    Show the answer

    Equal levels give the same 12,800 valid indices but not the same meaning: each codec learned its own mapping from index to sound. Every index is accepted and nothing raises, so you get fluent speech saying different words.

    From the Alaap guide, Part 5: Description → voice week 10, 5 h

    After this you can read the mapper code and the paper it copies, and explain the design choice in top_k=2.

    Guide 5.1 Mixture Density Networks 2 h

    Read Bishop, "Mixture Density Networks", 1994 (tech report, ~20 pages, very readable).

    Intuition a normal regressor predicts one output per input. But one description ("a warm low voice") corresponds to many valid voices. An MDN predicts a mixture of Gaussians instead of a point, so the model can say "any of these".

    Why it matters it is the difference between one voice per description and a family. The reference implementation is MDNLayer(256, 256, num_gaussians=10, dim_wise=True).

    Guide 5.2 PromptTTS++ 2 h the reference implementation

    Read Shimizu et al., "PromptTTS++: Controlling Speaker Identity in Prompt-Based Text-to-Speech Using Natural Language Descriptions", 2024. Then the code: line/promptttspp — Apache-2.0, weights downloadable.

    This is the only open working implementation of exactly the contract Alaap needs: natural-language description → speaker embedding → frozen TTS.

    Guide 5.3 Data-Speech and measure-first captions 1 h

    Read Lyth & King, "Natural language guidance of high-fidelity text-to-speech with synthetic annotations", 2024 (the Parler-TTS / Data-Speech line).

    Do compare against alaap/acoustics.py: Data-Speech computes 9 columns from 5 tools, equal-width bins. Alaap uses percentile bins and adds six attributes Data-Speech has not got. Read Binner's docstring for why percentile — it is a real finding about skewed corpora.

    Check Why does Binner regress HNR on log-F0 before binning it? (39.9% of HNR variance was pitch, a measurement artefact — and it made "a high, harsh voice" impossible to satisfy.)

    Exit check Why an MDN rather than a regressor that predicts one speaker vector?

    Show the answer

    Trained with squared error on a one-to-many mapping, a regressor predicts the average of every valid voice, which is a blurred central voice. An MDN predicts mixture weights, means and spreads, so sampling gives distinct plausible voices.

    Stage 18

    Evaluation, and why most of it is wrong

    about 5 h
    • Alaap guide 6.1
    • Alaap guide 6.2
    • Alaap guide 6.3
    • Alaap guide 6.4

    After this you can Design a measurement that will not fool you: the right diversity statistic, the right judge, and a listening test with its discard rule written first.

    Why it matters for Alaap This part has the highest ratio of hard-won knowledge to published literature in the whole project.

    From the Alaap guide, Part 6: Evaluation, and why most of it is wrong week 11, 5 h

    After this you can design a measurement that will not fool you. This is the part of the project with the highest ratio of hard-won knowledge to published literature.

    Guide 6.1 The MOS-predictor trap 1.5 h

    Read Reddy et al. DNSMOS (2021) and Saeki et al. UTMOS (2022), then RESEARCH/06-evaluation-harness.md §5.2.

    correlation with mean F0
    humans −0.059
    DNSMOS −0.788
    UTMOSv2 −0.722

    They also move less than 0.1 on prosodic corruption that costs humans 1.84 MOS points. For a project whose point is spanning the pitch range, a MOS gate systematically rejects high-pitched voices for a reason humans do not share. Invariant I9.

    Guide 6.2 Diversity: the Vendi score 1 h

    Read Friedman & Dieng, "The Vendi Score: A Diversity Evaluation Metric for Machine Learning", 2023.

    Intuition the exponential of the entropy of the eigenvalues of a similarity matrix. If you have 40 items that are really 20 distinct things, Vendi × n ≈ 20 — "effective voices".

    The trap this repo hit: normalised Vendi is a fraction of the maximum for a set of that size. 0.361 over 95 items and 0.362 over 38 are not the same thing — they are ~34 and ~14 effective voices. S9 retracted a published claim over this.

    Guide 6.3 Intelligibility 0.5 h

    WER/CER, ASR as a judge, and why CER not WER for Indic scripts.

    Guide 6.4 Listening tests 2 h read the skill, it is better than the literature

    Read .claude/skills/listening-tests/SKILL.md, then experiments/S14-rate-control/RESULTS-S14c.md as a worked failure.

    The compressed lessons:

    • Comparative, not single-stimulus, when the baseline is itself imperfect
    • Positive and negative controls, always
    • Write the discard condition down before sending the set — then honour it
    • Compute the false-positive rate of that condition. S14c's fired on a coin flip
    • Ask "does this say X?", never "does this sound right?"

    Check Design a test for "does the rate knob sound processed?" without letting the listener answer on clip length. (There is a real tension here; S14b and S14c both failed it in opposite ways.)

    Exit check Why would a MOS predictor make a bad naturalness gate for Alaap?

    Show the answer

    DNSMOS correlates with mean pitch at r = -0.788 where humans correlate at -0.059, so it systematically rejects high-pitched voices for a reason people do not share, fighting the diversity the project exists to create.

    Reflection questions from the module (5)
    1. Cache Size Calculation. A 12-layer transformer has 12 attention heads per layer, 64-dimensional embeddings per head,
    2. Speed vs Memory Trade-off. Your KVCache makes generation 10× faster but uses several GB of RAM.
    3. Batch Inference Scaling. Batch size 1 generates at 500 tokens/sec, using 50 MB cache. With KV cache, each sequence in a batch gets its own cache storage.
    4. Cache Eviction for Long Conversations. Your `KVCache` has `max_seq_len=2048`. A chatbot conversation reaches 2048 tokens - the cache is full!
    5. Production Reality - Multi-User Serving. ChatGPT serves millions of users. Each user's conversation needs its own KV cache.

    Exit check Why does a KV cache make autoregressive generation faster, and what does it cost?

    Show the answer

    Without it, each new token recomputes keys and values for the whole prefix, so generation is quadratic. The cache stores them and computes only the new token's, making each step linear. The cost is memory per sequence, which grows with length and limits how many users one GPU serves.

      Exit check Why does invariant I4 call a licence declaration a claim, not evidence?

      Show the answer

      Because derived models inherit their parents' terms, and the declaration on the derived model is often wrong: every one of the five Indic chains checked was mis-declared upstream. Only tracing the chain to the training data is evidence.

      The five ideas that took this project longest to learn

      If you remember nothing else:

      1. A suspiciously good or suspiciously bad number is a bug report about your setup. Recorded ~17 times here. Every single time.

      2. State the property before you read the result. Otherwise you will rationalise.

      3. An axis that fails to separate is a bug in the estimator until proven otherwise. Two "noise" axes turned out to be broken measurements.

      4. Effect size is not significance. A gap of 8 points with a standard error of 6 is nothing, and it will look like a finding.

      5. A metric is validated on a corpus, not in the abstract. Re-run the validation when the corpus, model, or codec changes.

      These are the three project skills in .claude/skills/ — statistical-claims, speech-feature-pitfalls, listening-tests. Read them at week 1 and again at week 13; they will mean different things.

      Exit check A new result is suspiciously good. What do you do first?

      Show the answer

      Treat it as a bug report about the setup. State the property you expected before reading further, then check the measurement, the corpus and the comparison: the project recorded this about seventeen times, every time.

      If you only have 10 hours, not 65

      The ruthless subset, in order:

      1. Part 0 (2 h) — orientation and the demo
      2. §2.3 source–filter (1 h) — nothing else in audio makes sense without it
      3. §3.3 the three navigability papers (3 h) — the intellectual core
      4. §4.2 neural codecs (2 h) — why modern TTS is a language model
      5. §6.1 + §6.4 the evaluation traps (2 h) — what stops you fooling yourself

      That gets you able to follow any conversation about this project. It does not get you able to change an experiment — that needs Part 1.

      Sanity check — where Alaap actually is, 2026-09-09

      Measured against RESEARCH/GRAND-PLAN.md, not against memory. Seven days. 143 commits. 35 experiments. 13 ADRs. 135 invariant tests.

      The one-line answer

      The direction vector is right. The magnitude has all gone into one component, and the plan named that failure mode in writing before it happened.

      Nothing here is wrong work. Almost none of it is product work.

      1. Stage-by-stage, against the plan's own exit criteria

      # Stage Exit criterion (plan's words) Status
      S0 Foundations + 10 experiments E1 returns g2s ≈ s2s, scorecard populated, corpus licence-cleared, every render watermarked 7/10 — E1–E5, E9 ✓ (+ E10–E15 extra). E6, E7, E8 never run
      S1 Voice identity persists Same character across 20 lines + restart + backend bump ✓ done, verified on hardware
      S2 Retrieval mapper Beats S0 on adherence at equal-or-better diversity ✓ done
      S3 Generative mapper (MDN → diffusion) Beats S2 on adherence × diversity jointly ✗ not started
      S4 Dataset v2 Attributes verifiable by re-measurement ◐ partial — Indic captions only
      S5 Indic gate Explicit go/no-go ✓ passed — then eight more experiments past it
      S6 Inference service mint + render over HTTP, ≥2 backends, no client change ✗ not started
      S7 GPU hosting p95 latency + $/min measured under load ✗ not started
      S8 Web app A stranger mints a voice unaided ✗ not started
      S9/S10 Multi-tenant, public release — ✗ not started

      alaap/service.py exists and works — but VoiceService is an in-process Python class. S6's criterion is over HTTP. That one word is the entire gap between here and a product.

      The minimum shippable thing is blocked, at its first step

      The plan defines MST = S0 + S1 + S6 + S7 + cut-down S8, and says of it:

      "Protect it. The most likely failure mode of this project is that S2/S3 research swallows the calendar and nothing ever ships."

      S0 ✓ and S1 ✓ are done. S6, S7, S8 have zero commits.

      2. Where the effort actually went

        experiments/  E0 E1 E2 E3 E4 E5 E9 E10 E11 E12 E13 E14 E15
                S2 S4 S5 S6 S7 S8 S9 S10 S11 S12 S13 S14 S15
                S16 S17 S18 S19 S20 S21 S22 S23 S24
                └────────────── 35 ──────────────┘

      A naming collision hides the gap. experiments/S6…S10 are Indic experiments. The plan's S6–S10 are the platform track. Day to day the directories look like progress through the stages; they are not the same S6.

      The last eight experiments are measurement-of-measurement

      what it produced
      S17 dropped 2 dead axes, repaired vtl_cm
      S18 audited all 17 attributes — no new axis helps
      S19 naturalness deficit splits evenly, codec vs model
      S20/S20b built the first naturalness gate; then corrected its own layer
      S21 spectral_tilt reads pitch — kept anyway
      S22 adopted the S17/S18 axis set (the one shipped change)
      S23 the gate's layer doesn't transfer; two of S20b's checks were wrong
      S24 repairing tilt makes it redundant with f0_mean

      Six of those eight outputs are caveats, not capabilities. They are honest, rigorous, and four of them found genuine bugs. They also do not move a user any closer to a voice.

      3. The steelman — why this was not wasted

      Stated fairly, because the case is real:

      1. Every one was justified when started. The catalogue saturates at ~22 effective voices; that is the MST's core number; finding out why is legitimate product work.

      2. Four audits found real bugs. vtl_cm was broken. speaking_rate/f0_cv were never identity axes. The gate's layer was wrong for English. S20b's pitch check was confounded. A pipeline shipping those would have been quietly wrong.

      3. Invariant I8 demanded it: "Do not start stage N+1 until stage N's exit criterion is measured." The measurement discipline is the plan's, not a deviation from it.

      4. The tests and skills are durable. 135 invariant tests and three project skills encode what was learned; the next person does not re-make these mistakes.

      The rebuttal is timing, not value. The question "can description-driven minting exceed ~22 effective voices?" was answered no several experiments ago, and the answer has been re-confirmed by increasingly indirect means since.

      4. The finding that should change the plan

      ! CORRECTED 2026-09-19 — the original compared two different quantities

      It read "retrieval reaches 87% adherence where minting reaches 58%". Invalid. S8's 87.3% is retrieval accuracy within one bin (exact-bin: 65.6%); S17's 58% is the "of bound" column, a diversity share — adherence in that same row is 95.8%. Accuracy was compared against diversity, which is the error statistical-claims §5 names. On adherence, minting is the MORE accurate of the two.

      S25 settled it properly. The corrected case is below, and it is stronger.

      The right comparison is capacity, on the same corpus, same embedding space, same statistic minting is scored on:

      effective voices
      minting, adopted axis set (S22, confirmed on hardware by S7) 22.3
      retrieval, 141 real Hindi speakers (S25) 38.4

      And it is the only lever that scales. Library size moves the number where nothing else did — effective ≈ n^0.49 over 20–141 speakers:

      library 20 40 80 141
      effective voices 14.7 22.7 32.1 38.4

      A library of ~40 real speakers already equals everything minting achieves. Against the four minting levers, all measured, all flat: novelty (S9), corpus size (S7), bins (S18), axes (S18).

      The honest trade: minting is more accurate (94.6% vs 65.6% exact), retrieval is more diverse (38.4 vs 22.3), needs no mapper, clears no floors, rejects nothing, and ships the original recording rather than synthesis.

      The real risk is not accuracy — it is licensing. Serving a voice derived from an identifiable real speaker is a different legal question from serving a synthesised one (I6, RESEARCH/09, the Arijit Singh line). IndicVoices-R is CC-BY-4.0 for the data; that is not a personality-rights clearance. This gates the whole re-scoping.

      5. Course correction

      Ordered by value per unit of effort. Updated 2026-09-19 — item 1 is done.

      # Action Cost Status
      1 ~~S6 — wrap VoiceService in an HTTP API.~~ ~1 day ✓ DONE — alaap/api.py, 6 tests, licence gate refuses at construction
      2 ~~Re-scope the catalogue to retrieval over corpus speakers.~~ ~2 days ✗ KILLED — ADR-013. CC-BY-4.0 §2(b)(1) does not license personality rights, and the waiver covers only the licensor's own. A servable catalogue needs licensed voices.
      3 ~~E8 — real $/min on short lines.~~ — ✓ DONE, $0 spent. RTF 5.01; short-line penalty +1.4% vs the model's ~12%; $0.028–$0.084/min single-stream. Concurrency still needs the rented GPU.
      4 Cut-down S8 — a page that lists voices and renders a line. ~3 days "A stranger mints a voice unaided" is the exit criterion; a chooser + render box meets it.
      5 Freeze estimator auditing. — Two consecutive audits (S21, S24) concluded "keep what ships". The lever is closed.

      Deliberately NOT next

      • S3 / E6 — the generative mapper. If the catalogue ships on retrieval, minting is a v2 feature. E6 (does PromptTTS++'s MDN give diverse voices?) stops being a blocker.

      • E7 — speaker count × session diversity. Corpus sizing only matters if the corpus is the constraint. S7 tested 141 → 432 speakers for zero change in effective voices.

      • More listening tests on rate control. S14d is built and waiting; after it, stop.

      What would change this recommendation

      • If S14d shows the rate artefact is badly asymmetric, Direction.rate needs rework before any service ships it.

      • If a library of 100–200 curated voices turns out to be hard to source under a clean licence, the retrieval reframing collapses and minting is back on the critical path. I4 says assume nothing here: five licence chains were mis-declared out of five checked.

      • If VPC 2026 results (2026-09-26) show synthetic-speaker generation solved the diversity problem, S3 gets cheap and interesting again.

      6. Honest scorecard
      Research quality Genuinely high. Pre-committed properties, controls for controls, corrections written into the file that was wrong.
      Engineering quality 135 invariant tests, 16 modules, no orphaned code.
      Scientific honesty Unusually good — several published claims were retracted by later experiments in the same repo.
      Product progress Stalled at the S1/S6 boundary for the entire project.
      Plan adherence High on Track A, zero on Track B, which the plan says starts at S1.

      Verdict: not a tangent — an over-investment. The work is on the right axis; it has been pushed far past the point where the next unit of measurement changes a decision. The plan's own hedge (ship the catalogue) is untouched, and the evidence now says that hedge is easier than it looked, because retrieval already works.

      Can we build "an old Australian man"? — three research passes

      Date: 2026-09-19 · three parallel web-research passes, primary sources Prompted by: the product goal being restated as description → voice, spanning *accent, age and emotion at the extremes — "an old Australian man", "a young Indian boy", "a husky Texan", "a naive Nigerian man".

      The three passes were independent and they converge on the same wall from three different sides. Not legal advice; enough to plan with.

      0 · The finding that starts it

      Accent does not exist anywhere in this system. Clip carries an accent field. It is not an axis, not a bin, not a caption phrase, and not in any cached attribute set — the 2,500-clip GLOBE_V2 cache holds acoustic scalars only. Same for age.

      The current axis set is f0_mean, spectral_tilt, vtl_cm — pitch, brightness, vocal-tract length. None of the four target descriptions can be expressed in it.

      And the escape hatch people reach for does not apply: S18's "no new axis ever helps" was an audit of 17 acoustic scalars. Accent is categorical and phonetic, not a percentile bin. It was never in that audit, so the ~22-effective-voice ceiling does not rule it out.

      1 · Technical — can a frozen TTS be given accent control?

      The short answer: only one mechanism is architecturally compatible, and it is not an axis

      mechanism works with a FROZEN TTS? used by
      categorical accent ID → embedding table ✗ trained jointly with the acoustic model standard multi-accent baselines
      disentangled accent encoder (GRL / ML-VAE+VQ) ✗ needs joint training Joycent, DART
      accent-intensity subspace ! partial — subspace itself is jointly trained CrossAccent-TTS
      codec-level factorisation ! only if your codec is already factorised FAC-FACodec
      text/phoneme-side transliteration ✓ yes — modifies the input, not the model MacST
      reference-audio-driven ✓ but accent rides along with the whole identity any zero-shot cloner
      description → x-vector distribution (MDN) ✓ this is our architecture ProPS

      Accent is entangled with speaker identity, by construction

      Each accent is represented by multiple speakers, but each speaker has one accent. Accent and identity are therefore correlated in any corpus.

      Every system that achieves good accent/speaker separation does it with a jointly-trained adversarial or hierarchical objective — Joycent's gradient reversal, DART's ML-VAE+VQ. That is exactly the retraining a frozen TTS rules out.

      No paper found claims accent is cleanly linearly separable in an arbitrary pretrained speaker embedding the way f0_mean and vtl_cm are.

      Three negative data points that matter to us specifically
      PromptTTS++ — our reference implementation its speaker-prompt vocabulary is gender-neutral / young / old / muffled. No accent.
      Data-Speech — the annotation pipeline we compare against does not annotate accent. Parler-TTS handles accent by prompt-engineered generalisation, not a trained axis
      Audiobox (Meta), in its own paper CLAP-style joint audio-text embeddings "frequently fall short in capturing intricate attributes such as accents"

      The one paper to read

      ProPS — natural-language profile → sentence embedding → mixture-density network → Gaussian mixture in x-vector space, explicitly conditioning on age, gender, accent and prosody. Architecturally almost identical to this project's mapper, and it is the only found system doing description→accent into a frozen downstream. It does not solve entanglement; it gives a principled way to sample an embedding given a description.

      (S3 in the plan is "MDN → two-stage diffusion". ProPS is an MDN. These are the same experiment, and S3 was never started.)

      The gap nobody has measured — and we are positioned to

      Does accent conditioning survive emotion conditioning? The literature has nothing.

      • E0's task-vector work: emotion is localised to the x-vector and applied additively (x + α·τ) with speaker identity retained at SECS ≥ 0.88. But their base vector is accent-unmarked.

      • DUET found emotion "nearly orthogonal to speaker identity" in frozen hidden states — orthogonal to identity, which is not the same as orthogonal to accent, and accent and identity are entangled with each other.

      Nobody has stacked accent and emotion offsets and measured the interaction. We have the τ machinery already working. That is a real, publishable, cheap question.

      Corpora, for scale

      corpus accents speakers
      VCTK 11–13 109
      L2-ARCTIC 6 L1 groups 24
      GLOBE_V2 164 23,519

      We already use GLOBE_V2 and we use 2,500 clips of it with the accent labels discarded.

      2 · Rights — can we serve voices built from any of it?

      Of 19 corpora audited, not one has speaker-facing consent naming synthesis, cloning, voice generation, or TTS-model training. This is ADR-013 generalising from IndicVoices-R to the whole field.

      corpus licence consent names synthesis? accents speakers
      CMU ARCTIC BSD-style closest to yes — signed waiver, "voice talents", built for synthesis, but the waiver text never says the word 4 labelled ~18
      IndicVoices-R CC-BY-4.0 no — real IRB-reviewed consent, but generic "potential uses of their data" 22 languages 10,496
      VCTK ! conflict: ODC-By on DataShare vs CC-BY-4.0 on the HF mirror — unresolved purpose in the title only yes, per speaker 110
      GLOBE_V2 CC0 no — inherits Common Voice 164 23,519
      Common Voice CC0 (no longer universal) no — Mozilla's ToU names only "speech-to-text technology" yes, self-reported tens of thousands

      CC0's own deed says it does not cover "publicity or privacy rights… how their voice… is used" — the same structural point as CC-BY-4.0 §2(b)(1) in ADR-013. A CC0 tag is not a voice clearance either.

      Do not use: Emilia (scraped, zero consent, NC), L2-ARCTIC (NC), EARS (NC), DAPS (NC), Expresso (NC), VoxPopuli (named politicians, no opt-in), SpeechOcean762 (child speakers), Snow Mountain (unresolved chain).

      3 · Commercial — can we just buy voices?

      No — and the reason is structural, not financial.

      Nobody sells the embedding. Everyone sells API access.

      Across ElevenLabs (Voice Library and Iconic Marketplace), Respeecher, Veritone, Altered, WellSaid, Murf, Sarvam, Deepdub, Papercup, TTS.ai — every one delivers finished audio from their own hosted model. Respeecher's ToS explicitly bars deriving model components; TTS.ai explicitly bars redistributing the voice asset. Several (Murf, ElevenLabs) explicitly forbid using outputs to train any model.

      This is incompatible with a frozen-TTS architecture that drives its own model from a speaker embedding. "Licensing a voice" in this market means licensing the right to call their endpoint.

      Two gaps worth a real contract read rather than a marketing page: Respeecher and Veritone enterprise tiers (Veritone custom voice model from $9,000/voice; terms not public), and a bespoke deal via Voices.com / Voice123, where you license a performer's consent directly and could in principle negotiate embedding delivery.

      Union frameworks (SAG-AFTRA, NAVA's fAIrVoices rider) set consent floors; they do not sell anything. NAVA's rider prohibits AI training without explicit sign-off.

      4 · What this means

      The three walls are one wall

      1. The accent diversity we want (GLOBE_V2, 164 accents) has no synthesis consent.
      2. We cannot buy synthesis-cleared embeddings — nobody sells them.
      3. Accent cannot be a clean fourth axis in a frozen TTS's speaker embedding.

      But measuring is not serving, and that is the whole opening

      ADR-013's own distinction: IndicVoices-R stays cleared for fitting the space, anchoring geometry and measuring bounds — because those do not serve an identity. The same applies to GLOBE_V2's 164 accents.

      So the next experiment is free of every wall above:

      ✓ ANSWERED 2026-09-19 — NO. S26 and S27.

      Two corpora, two label regimes, one and three clips per speaker, same encoder: gender lifts +13.9 then +46.7 points; accent lifts +1.0 then +4.0. The positive control goes to 100% accuracy while accent stays at noise. Four of the five mechanisms below operate on the speaker embedding and therefore have nothing to work with. Text-side transliteration is the only route left — which was already the only one a frozen TTS can accept.

      Does accent separate at all in the Qwen3 speaker-embedding space? Stream GLOBE_V2 with its accent labels, run the same within/between screen every axis in this project has faced, and find out whether accent is even there to be controlled before any product decision depends on it.

      If accent does not separate in this embedding space, the whole direction is dead and we know in an afternoon. If it does, the questions become which mechanism (§1) and which cleared voices (§2) — in that order.

      The honest ceiling, stated now

      Accent cannot be added the way vtl_cm was. The literature's best accent control needs joint training, which the two-tower thesis forbids. The realistic ceilings are:

      route cost what it buys
      text-side transliteration (MacST) days the only guaranteed-compatible mechanism; unknown whether Qwen3 responds
      reference-clip accent bank medium accent rides with a whole identity, not separable
      categorical accent offset in the embedding medium will move accent AND identity; magnitude untested
      ProPS-style MDN mapper medium-high principled sampling, same entanglement
      full adversarial disentanglement ruled out requires training the TTS

      And one thing we could contribute

      Nobody has measured whether accent and emotion conditioning interact. We have E0's τ vectors working and the machinery to stack them. It is cheap, it is unanswered, and it is directly on the product's path.

      Sources

      Every claim above traces to a primary source read during the research passes — CC0 and CC-BY-4.0 legal deeds, Mozilla's Terms of Use and Privacy Notice (eff. 2025-10-31), the IndicVoices/IndicVoices-R papers, CMU ARCTIC's waiver, provider ToS pages, and the accent papers named inline. Where a source could not be reached (VCTK's DataShare licence file 404'd; Veritone's custom-voice terms), that is stated rather than inferred.
